focus: heart failure, shock, disposition, and mechanical support

questions.learning_objective: Avoid reflexive large-volume resuscitation when shock coexists with pulmonary/systemic congestion and severe ventricular dysfunction.
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with suspected myocarditis is hypotensive with cool extremities and delayed capillary refill. Examination also shows hepatomegaly and pulmonary crackles; echocardiography shows severely depressed LV function. A sepsis pathway proposes repeated rapid crystalloid boluses. What is the best response?

options.text: Define preload and congestion, use only cautious reassessed fluid if truly needed, and escalate cardiogenic-shock support
Give repeated large rapid boluses until the blood pressure normalizes
Withhold all circulatory support until myocarditis is biopsy confirmed
Replace the IV resuscitation plan with unrestricted oral hydration
Give diuretic therapy alone and ignore poor perfusion because pulmonary congestion is present

questions.rationale: The child has both low output and congestion, making pump failure—not simple volume depletion—the dominant physiology. Additional fluid can worsen filling pressures and pulmonary edema; management requires reassessment and hemodynamic support tailored to the phenotype.

option_explanations.cautious_reassess: Correct. Small amounts of fluid may occasionally be appropriate if preload is inadequate, but the default in congested cardiogenic shock is not repeated empiric volume loading.
option_explanations.repeat_bolus: Tempting because pediatric shock pathways often start with fluid, but the demonstrated congestion and severe LV dysfunction make repeated large boluses potentially harmful. Aggressive fluid is more appropriate when true hypovolemia is the dominant physiology and congestion is absent.
option_explanations.no_support: Etiologic certainty should not delay shock treatment. Biopsy is selective and can occur only after immediate perfusion threats are addressed.
option_explanations.oral_fluids: Oral hydration cannot correct cardiogenic shock and may worsen congestion. It is appropriate only in stable patients with uncomplicated volume depletion and intact cardiac reserve.
option_explanations.diuretic_only: Congestion matters, but this child also has shock and poor systemic perfusion. Decongestion must be integrated with support of cardiac output and blood pressure rather than treated in isolation.

questions.board_pearl: Before giving fluid in shock, ask whether the child is empty—or failing to pump.

evidence.claim: Pediatric acute decompensated heart failure management requires assessment of congestion and perfusion before fluid decisions.
Fulminant myocarditis can cause cardiogenic shock requiring urgent hemodynamic support.

questions.learning_objective: Choose vasoactive/inotropic support according to blood pressure and perfusion rather than assume one universal myocarditis drug.
questions.stem: A 9-year-old with fulminant myocarditis has persistent low cardiac output despite careful preload optimization. Which general vasoactive principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Select inotropic and/or vasopressor support according to the child's blood pressure, systemic vascular tone, perfusion, and ventricular function
Use the same single vasoactive drug in every child with myocarditis regardless of hemodynamics
Avoid vasoactive agents and continue escalating fluids until perfusion improves
Do not support blood pressure or contractility until biopsy confirms myocarditis
Treat the heart rate alone because perfusion will normalize automatically

questions.rationale: There is no one-size-fits-all vasoactive regimen for pediatric myocarditis. Support should match the hemodynamic phenotype: contractility, blood pressure, systemic vascular tone, and end-organ perfusion.

option_explanations.phenotype_support: Correct. Hemodynamic phenotype drives whether the child needs more contractile support, vascular tone support, or both, with repeated reassessment.
option_explanations.one_drug: A universal agent ignores major differences between hypotensive, vasoconstricted, vasodilated, or relatively normotensive low-output states. Specific drug selection belongs to critical-care/cardiology management based on the phenotype.
option_explanations.fluids_replace: Fluids cannot correct severe pump failure and may worsen congestion. They are useful only when preload is genuinely inadequate.
option_explanations.wait_biopsy: Shock treatment cannot wait for pathology. Diagnostic clarification and physiologic support proceed in parallel.
option_explanations.rate_only: Heart rate can be compensatory or pathologic, but cardiac output depends on more than rate. Treating a number without the hemodynamic mechanism can worsen the child.

questions.board_pearl: In myocarditis shock, treat hemodynamics—not a favorite vasoactive drug.

evidence.claim: Pediatric ADHF/cardiogenic shock management is hemodynamically individualized and evidence for one universal vasoactive regimen is limited.
Fulminant myocarditis may require inotropic/vasopressor and mechanical circulatory support.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize that airway/ventilation decisions in severe myocardial dysfunction can change preload and hemodynamics and require coordinated critical-care planning.
questions.stem: A 6-year-old with severe myocarditis has worsening pulmonary edema, fatigue, and hypoxemia while blood pressure is falling and perfusion is poor. Which approach to respiratory support is best?

options.text: Escalate respiratory support as needed while planning induction and positive-pressure ventilation as a high-risk hemodynamic event with cardiac/critical-care support
Avoid all positive-pressure ventilation because it is absolutely contraindicated in myocarditis
Give deep sedation without a coordinated airway or circulatory plan
Delay treatment of respiratory failure until CMR defines the extent of inflammation
Encourage ambulation to recruit lung volume and improve oxygenation

questions.rationale: Respiratory failure must be treated, but induction and positive pressure can alter venous return, vascular resistance, and blood pressure in a child with little cardiac reserve. Airway and circulatory planning should occur together.

option_explanations.coordinated_airway: Correct. The point is not to avoid ventilation but to anticipate cardiovascular collapse and ensure monitoring, vasoactive support, skilled airway personnel, and advanced-support readiness.
option_explanations.avoid_vent: Positive-pressure ventilation is not absolutely contraindicated; untreated respiratory failure is dangerous. Avoidance becomes harmful when the child can no longer maintain oxygenation or ventilation.
option_explanations.sedate_only: Sedation can reduce sympathetic tone and blood pressure and should not be given as a substitute for definitive respiratory/hemodynamic management. It belongs within a deliberate airway plan when needed.
option_explanations.wait_cmr: Advanced imaging must never delay stabilization of respiratory or circulatory failure.
option_explanations.exercise: Active myocarditis with respiratory failure and shock is incompatible with exercise; exertion would increase metabolic demand and risk.

questions.board_pearl: In severe myocarditis, an airway intervention is also a cardiovascular intervention.

evidence.claim: Pediatric acute heart failure can rapidly progress and requires coordinated management of respiratory and circulatory failure.
Fulminant myocarditis requires anticipatory multidisciplinary critical-care management.

questions.learning_objective: Trigger transfer to an ECMO/MCS-capable center before irreversible end-organ failure or cardiac arrest develops.
questions.stem: An 8-year-old with suspected myocarditis has worsening biventricular function, rising lactate, oliguria, and increasing vasoactive needs at a hospital without pediatric mechanical circulatory support. What is the best systems-level decision?

options.text: Activate transfer to a pediatric ECMO/MCS-capable cardiac center while stabilization continues
Wait until cardiac arrest occurs because transfer is only indicated after conventional support fails completely
Continue care on a general ward because myocarditis often recovers spontaneously
Arrange next-day pediatric cardiology follow-up if the oxygen saturation remains normal
Require local biopsy confirmation before discussing transfer

questions.rationale: Progressive low-output shock and end-organ dysfunction in myocarditis are pre-arrest findings. Pediatric resuscitation guidance recommends early ICU/advanced-center escalation and transfer when refractory low output may require ECMO/MCS.

option_explanations.transfer_now: Correct. Transfer logistics are safer and more useful before refractory shock becomes arrest or multiorgan failure.
option_explanations.wait_arrest: Waiting for arrest sacrifices the window for planned transport and advanced support. ECPR may be reasonable in arrest, but prevention of arrest is preferable.
option_explanations.ward: Spontaneous recovery occurs, but this child is deteriorating and needs resources a general ward cannot provide.
option_explanations.outpatient: Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude low cardiac output. Oliguria, lactate rise, and escalating support are incompatible with outpatient management.
option_explanations.biopsy_before: Tissue diagnosis can matter, but transfer and stabilization should not be delayed for a local invasive procedure when the child may need MCS.

questions.board_pearl: Transfer for myocarditis should be triggered by trajectory—not by cardiac arrest.

evidence.claim: Early transfer to a center with ECMO/MCS capability is reasonable in pediatric myocarditis/cardiomyopathy with refractory low cardiac output.
Anticipatory transfer to advanced pediatric cardiovascular care is central to myocarditis management.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize temporary MCS as a bridge to recovery in refractory fulminant myocarditis rather than a declaration that transplantation is inevitable.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old with fulminant myocarditis remains in refractory low-output shock despite intensive medical therapy and is placed on VA-ECMO. Which counseling statement is most accurate?

options.text: Temporary mechanical support may preserve end-organ perfusion while native myocardial function recovers; some children will still require durable support or transplantation
VA-ECMO means heart transplantation is inevitable
Severe shock makes meaningful ventricular recovery impossible
If ventricular function recovers on ECMO, no later cardiac follow-up is needed
Mechanical support removes the risk of ventricular arrhythmias

questions.rationale: Fulminant myocarditis can show substantial native myocardial recovery when circulation is supported through the acute phase. MCS is often a bridge to recovery, but outcomes vary and some children require VAD or transplant.

option_explanations.bridge_recovery: Correct. This is the central rationale for early temporary support in a potentially reversible inflammatory cardiomyopathy.
option_explanations.transplant_all: Some children require transplantation, but many recover native function. Transplant becomes necessary when recovery is inadequate or other factors dictate durable support.
option_explanations.recovery_impossible: Severe initial presentation does not preclude recovery; pediatric ECMO cohorts document rapid and durable recovery in many survivors.
option_explanations.no_followup: Recovery from the acute shock phase does not erase residual scar, rhythm risk, or recurrence concerns. Longitudinal cardiology follow-up remains important.
option_explanations.no_arrhythmia: ECMO supports circulation but does not eliminate myocardial electrical instability. Rhythm monitoring continues during support.

questions.board_pearl: Fulminant myocarditis can be both catastrophically ill and highly recoverable—MCS buys time for that recovery.

evidence.claim: ECMO/MCS can benefit children with myocarditis/cardiomyopathy and refractory low cardiac output.
Contemporary pediatric fulminant myocarditis ECMO cohorts demonstrate substantial transplant-free myocardial recovery among survivors.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize arrhythmia, heart block, low output, and organ failure as pre-arrest features that justify ICU escalation even before frank arrest.
questions.stem: Which new finding in a hospitalized 13-year-old with myocarditis most clearly indicates a pre-arrest state requiring immediate ICU-level escalation?

options.text: New high-grade AV block with hypotension and signs of low cardiac output
Mild improving chest discomfort with stable vital signs
Return of normal appetite
Persistent rhinorrhea after the antecedent viral illness
Stable sinus rhythm with improving ventricular function

questions.rationale: Pediatric resuscitation guidance identifies heart block, ventricular arrhythmia, low cardiac output, respiratory support needs, and organ failure in myocarditis as high-risk pre-arrest features.

option_explanations.high_grade_block_low_output: Correct. Electrical and hemodynamic instability together create an immediate risk of progression to cardiac arrest.
option_explanations.mild_chest_pain: Chest pain is important but does not by itself define pre-arrest physiology when hemodynamics and rhythm are stable.
option_explanations.normal_appetite: Improving general symptoms are reassuring but do not independently determine cardiac risk.
option_explanations.isolated_rhinorrhea: This may reflect the preceding infection and is not an acute cardiac instability marker.
option_explanations.stable_sinus: Stable rhythm with improving function describes recovery rather than impending arrest.

questions.board_pearl: In myocarditis, heart block or ventricular arrhythmia plus low output should be treated as pre-arrest physiology.

evidence.claim: Arrhythmias, heart block, ST changes, low cardiac output, invasive ventilation needs, and organ failure are high-risk/pre-arrest findings in pediatric myocarditis.

questions.learning_objective: Differentiate congestion without shock from low-output shock and avoid treating every decompensated child with either fluids or vasoactives by default.
questions.stem: A 5-year-old with myocarditis has tachypnea, hepatomegaly, and pulmonary congestion but is alert, normotensive, warm, and has preserved urine output. Which principle best fits the immediate management?

options.text: Treat congestion and monitor closely for deterioration rather than reflexively giving large fluid boluses or shock-level vasoactive therapy
Treat as refractory cardiogenic shock solely because pulmonary edema is present
Give repeated large rapid crystalloid boluses because all tachycardia implies volume depletion
Discharge because warm extremities exclude significant heart failure
Use exercise to improve ventricular conditioning during the active illness

questions.rationale: The child is congested but not currently showing shock physiology. Management intensity should match the hemodynamic phenotype, with decongestive/supportive heart-failure care and close monitoring because myocarditis can evolve rapidly.

option_explanations.decongest_monitor: Correct. Congestion and perfusion are separate axes; a warm, perfused child does not need shock treatment solely because fluid overload is present.
option_explanations.shock_vasoactive: Vasoactive support is appropriate when cardiac output or blood pressure is inadequate. Pulmonary congestion alone does not prove refractory shock.
option_explanations.large_fluid: The child is already congested, making repeated fluid loading physiologically mismatched. Fluids belong in true preload deficiency, not indiscriminately in every tachycardic child.
option_explanations.discharge: Warm perfusion is reassuring but does not erase active myocarditis with pulmonary and systemic congestion. Ongoing monitoring and treatment are still needed.
option_explanations.exercise: Exercise is restricted during active myocarditis and is not a decongestive therapy.

questions.board_pearl: Separate congestion from perfusion: a child can be 'wet and warm' without being in shock.

evidence.claim: Pediatric acute decompensated heart failure is managed by defining congestion and perfusion and matching treatment intensity to the phenotype.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize biventricular dysfunction as a higher-risk finding that affects monitoring and transfer decisions.
questions.stem: An 11-year-old with suspected myocarditis has moderate LV dysfunction and newly recognized RV dysfunction with worsening hepatomegaly. Why does the RV finding matter?

options.text: It suggests more extensive pump involvement and can increase concern for hemodynamic deterioration
RV dysfunction rules out myocarditis because myocarditis affects only the LV
RV dysfunction proves pulmonary embolism
RV function has no bearing on monitoring or risk if the LV ejection fraction is known
RV dysfunction is expected physiologic remodeling in all active children

questions.rationale: Myocarditis can involve both ventricles. Biventricular dysfunction reflects broader myocardial involvement and should heighten attention to congestion, perfusion, and advanced-support needs.

option_explanations.greater_extent: Correct. RV performance contributes materially to cardiac output and systemic venous congestion and should be integrated into severity assessment.
option_explanations.rules_out: Myocarditis is not an LV-only disease; RV involvement is recognized.
option_explanations.proves_pe: Pulmonary embolism can cause RV dysfunction, but RV dysfunction alone is not diagnostic. PE becomes more likely with compatible risk factors and pulmonary vascular findings.
option_explanations.no_change: Ignoring the RV can underestimate severity, especially when systemic congestion is worsening.
option_explanations.athlete: Physiologic athletic remodeling is not synonymous with pathologic RV systolic dysfunction in an acutely ill child.

questions.board_pearl: Assess both ventricles; right-sided failure can be central to the myocarditis phenotype and disposition.

evidence.claim: Pediatric myocarditis may cause biventricular dysfunction and advanced heart failure.
Biventricular dysfunction is a higher-risk feature in contemporary myocarditis risk assessment.

questions.learning_objective: Use serial perfusion and end-organ trends to detect failed conventional support before arrest.
questions.stem: A 4-year-old with myocarditis and depressed ventricular function is receiving intensive care. Which trend most strongly indicates that current support is failing and escalation should accelerate?

options.text: Progressive oliguria, rising lactate, worsening mental status, and hepatic/renal injury
Falling troponin with stable perfusion
Resolution of the antecedent fever
Poor appetite without hemodynamic change
Normal oxygen saturation despite unchanged low-output findings

questions.rationale: Progressive end-organ injury signals sustained inadequate perfusion and a shrinking window for safe escalation. Serial physiology is more important than isolated improvement in fever or a myocardial biomarker.

option_explanations.organ_failure: Correct. End-organ dysfunction is evidence that low cardiac output is no longer being adequately compensated.
option_explanations.troponin_fall: A falling injury marker is encouraging but does not prove adequate perfusion or pump recovery. It would be reassuring only if hemodynamics and organ function also improve.
option_explanations.fever_resolves: Inflammatory symptoms can resolve while cardiac failure worsens; fever trajectory is not a sufficient marker of circulatory recovery.
option_explanations.appetite: Poor appetite is nonspecific and much less important than objective deterioration in perfusion and organ function.
option_explanations.normal_spo2: Pulse oximetry can remain normal in cardiogenic shock; it does not measure systemic blood flow.

questions.board_pearl: Do not wait for arrest: rising lactate and organ injury mean the circulation is already failing.

evidence.claim: Refractory low cardiac output and end-organ compromise in pediatric myocarditis should prompt early MCS/ECMO consideration and transfer.
Fulminant myocarditis requires early recognition of progressive shock and multiorgan failure.

questions.learning_objective: Recognize an ECMO complication that requires specialist management without testing general pediatricians on procedural technique.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old with fulminant myocarditis is already on VA-ECMO at a tertiary cardiac center. Echocardiography now shows progressive left-heart distention and pulmonary edema with poor aortic-valve opening. Which statement is most appropriate for a general-pediatrics board-level understanding?

options.text: This is an advanced mechanical-support problem that may require left-heart unloading/decompression by the ECMO/cardiac team
The appropriate response is unrestricted rapid fluid loading to increase LV filling further
LV distention is an expected harmless effect of VA-ECMO and needs no reassessment
Passive exercise is the preferred method to open the aortic valve
Improved systemic perfusion on ECMO permits discharge despite pulmonary edema

questions.rationale: VA-ECMO can increase LV afterload and produce left-heart distention, pulmonary edema, and poor native ejection. The general pediatrician should recognize the complication and need for specialist mechanical-support management; procedural selection is subspecialty care.

option_explanations.specialist_unloading: Correct. The core educational target is recognition and escalation, not choosing a specific venting technique.
option_explanations.fluid_bolus: Additional volume can worsen left-sided distention and pulmonary edema. Fluid may be needed in other ECMO states, but not as an automatic response to an already distended left heart.
option_explanations.ignore: Persistent LV distention can increase wall stress and thrombotic/pulmonary complications and therefore requires expert reassessment.
option_explanations.exercise: Exercise is irrelevant and unsafe in this critically ill mechanically supported patient.
option_explanations.discharge: ECMO is intensive life support; ongoing pulmonary edema and poor LV ejection require tertiary inpatient management.

questions.board_pearl: For ABP-level learning, recognize VA-ECMO LV distention as a specialist escalation problem; do not memorize a venting procedure.

evidence.claim: Left-heart decompression is a recognized advanced management issue in pediatric myocarditis/DCM supported with VA-ECMO.
